title: Lab 5: Interrupts
text:
The main goal of this lab was to measure the angular velocity and direction of a brushed DC motor using a quadrature encoder and interrupts on an STM32 microcontroller. We implemented an algorithm to count encoder pulses, calculated velocity and direction, and displayed the results to the user at an update rate of at least 1 Hz.






Schematic



Researched how to enable interrupts on the STM32 microcontroller, focusing on GPIO pin configuration and CMSIS library functions.
Configured an interrupt on a GPIO pin to detect pulses from the quadrature encoder.
Used a counter to count the number of interrupts and a timer to measure the time between pulses.
Calculated angular velocity based on the number of pulses per revolution and the time taken for each pulse.
Displayed the calculated velocity and direction to the screen using the printf function.





Verified interrupt functionality by printing a message to the screen when the interrupt was triggered.
Ensured accurate speed calculation by comparing results to the motor’s known speed of approximately 10 rev/s.
Tested the system at both high and low motor speeds to confirm consistent performance.





The design met all requirements. The system successfully calculated and displayed motor velocity and direction at a 1 Hz update rate.
No significant shortcomings were identified in the design, though time spent understanding documentation and interrupt setup delayed progress.




Approximately 12 hours were spent on this lab, including debugging and testing (replace X with your actual hours).

title: Lab 1: FPGA and MCU Setup and Testing
text: In this lab, a verilog module was implemented on the FPGA to control LEDs and interface with a 7-segment display. This lab demonstrates the ability to write modular verilog that interfaces with hardware, along with the ability to build, assemble, test, and debug circuits.

title: Lab 1: FPGA and MCU Setup and Testing
text: In this lab, a verilog module was implemented on the FPGA to control LEDs and interface with a 7-segment display. This lab demonstrates the ability to write modular verilog that interfaces with hardware, along with the ability to build, assemble, test, and debug circuits.

title: Lab 1: FPGA and MCU Setup and Testing
text:
Design and Testing Methodology
The on-board high-speed oscillator (HSOSC) from the iCE40 UltraPlus primitive library was used to generate a clock signal at 24MHz. Then, a counter was used to divide the high frequency clock signal down to a frequency of 2.4Hz which was then easily visualized using one of the on-board LEDs. We used the FPGA’s Programmable Logic Blocks (PLB) in order to drive two LEDs and our 7 segment display. LED0 followed the logic of a xor operation and LED1 followed the logic of an AND operation. The inputs of LED0 and LED1 were driven with 4 individual switches each assigned their own GPIO input pin and either outputted 3.3V logic. We then tested the logic of the 4 switches and ensured that our inputs aligned with the expected outputs.
The next step was to integrate the 7 segment display logic. Using the same 4 individual switches, they would encode a binary value from 0-15 which would be represented on our 7 segment display using Hexadecimal values 0-F. Upon reviewing the 7 Segment Display it was found that the model number was KYX-5101AS with a shared cathode. This meant there a shared 3.3v rail between all diodes, and each individual diode pin would have to be pulled to ground for current to form. Each diode was rated for 20 mA, so consequently 10mA was chosen as the target current. It was calculated that a 150 ohm resistor between each diode and ground would be sufficient. After this all GPIO pins were set to high (the default state of our combinational block) and each individual diode was prodded with a grounding wire to ensure each LED lit up appropriately without any unusual behavior. From this point on the Combinational Logic was programmed, GPIO pins were assigned, and the sequence of binary values from 0-15 were tested to see if the appropriate hexadecimal values 0-F were displayed.

title: Lab 1: FPGA and MCU Setup and Testing
text:
Technical Documentation:
The source code for the project can be found in the associated Github Repository.

Block Diagram



Figure 1: Block Diagram


The block diagram in Figure 1 demonstrates the overall architecture of the design. The top-level module lab_1 includes 3 submodules: - HZ_blink which drives an LED2 at 2.4Hz. - led_blink which drives LED0 and LED1 using combinational logic and our 4 switches as inputs. - seven_seg_display which drives our seven segment display using combinational logic and our 4 switches as inputs.


Schematic



Figure 2: Schematic


Figure 2 shows the physical layout of the design. Internal 100 \(k\ohm\) pullup resistors were use to ensure that the diodes defaulted to 3.3v as to not power on any diodes. In order to ensure that each LED on the 7 segment display maintained a 10mA of current again we used 150 \(\ohm\) resistored between the diode and our GPIO pins.

title: Lab 1: FPGA and MCU Setup and Testing
text:
Results and Discussion
At the conclusion of this lab I was able to display a set of hexadecimal numbers on a 7-Segment Display that was being driven by a 4 DIP switch module. In order to do this I learned how to incorporate combinational logic blocks in my verilog code, and also drove a set of LED’s with simple AND/OR logic depending on DIP switch positioning. I was also able to successfully make use of the onboard High Speed Oscillator (HSOC) in conjunction with a counter module to blink an on board LED at 2.4 Hz. Overly the completion of this lab demonstrates the ability to write modular verilog, along with the ability to build, assemble, test, and debug circuits.

title: Lab 1: FPGA and MCU Setup and Testing
text:
Testbench Simulation
 To verify the 7-Segment Display logic I forced our 4 bit s input to take on every value from 0-F in Hexadecimal. Upon reviewing the outputs of the seg variable I was able to verify that each output was as expected in our set of cases that I outlined. This was then further verified upon deployment of the verilog code to the FPGA. In future labs I plan on setting up a test bench environment for a more streamlined simulated verification process.

title: Lab 2: Multiplexed 7-Segment Display
text:
The primary objectives of this lab were to:

Implement a time-multiplexing scheme to drive two seven-segment displays using a single set of FPGA I/O pins.
Build a simple transistor circuit to handle the high current requirements of the seven-segment display’s common anodes.
Modularly design a Verilog system to display two hexadecimal numbers and their sum on FPGA outputs.

The final design successfully displayed two independent hexadecimal numbers on a dual seven-segment display, with the sum of the two numbers represented in binary on a set of five LEDs.



A modular design approach was implemented:



Netlist Analyzer





Schematic



Seven-Segment Decoder: Reused the seven-segment decoder module from the previous lab to drive the cathodes for hexadecimal digits.
Time-Multiplexing: A counter-based time-multiplexing scheme was used to switch between two input sources. The counter toggled between activating the left and right seven-segment displays by enabling their common anodes alternately.
Binary Addition: Combinational logic was employed to calculate the sum of the two 4-bit inputs. The result was output to the 5-bit LED array.
Transistor Circuit: A 2N3906 PNP transistor circuit was used to drive the common anodes of the seven-segment display to handle the higher current demands. Proper base current limiting resistors ensured no excessive current draw from the FPGA.







Verified the time-multiplexing logic in simulation to ensure proper alternation of the displays without bleeding or flicker.
Simulated the seven-segment decoder to confirm accurate encoding of hexadecimal values.
Checked combinational logic for correctness in binary addition.





Used DIP switches to input hexadecimal values and observed corresponding outputs on the displays.
Verified the stability and brightness of the displays to ensure proper operation of the transistor circuit.
Tested the sum displayed on the 5-bit LED array by changing input values and verifying expected results.








Both hexadecimal numbers were displayed correctly on the seven-segment display.
Time-multiplexing worked without noticeable flicker.
The sum of the two numbers was accurately displayed in binary on the LEDs.
Modular design principles were adhered to.





Due to the lack of a second 4-pin DIP switch, one input value was hard-coded for testing purposes. This limited the full flexibility of testing.





Approximately 6 hours were spent on this lab:

3 hours designing the Verilog modules.
3 hours testing and validating the implementation on hardware.

title: Lab 4: Digital Audio
text:
For this assignment, we were tasked with playing “Für Elise” over a speaker using an MCU. The main goals were to ensure the song played at the proper frequency and tempo while implementing timer functionality and audio amplification. My approach involved enabling the correct clock frequency, configuring timers, and generating PWM signals to drive a speaker through an LM386 amplifier. I spent approximately 10 hours completing this lab.






Schematic


My design approach was modular, starting with clock configuration and progressing to timer implementation:

Clock Configuration:

I enabled the PLL to achieve the desired system clock frequency.
The system clock was set to the default 4 MHz of the STM32 MCU, which I used as a basis for timer calculations.

Timer Configuration:

Configured Timer 2 to generate a PWM output.

Configured Timer 6 as a counter for timing durations.

PWM Signal Generation:

Timer 2’s PWM output was connected to a GPIO pin driving the speaker.

I implemented a function to adjust Timer 2’s registers to set the PWM frequency dynamically based on the note’s pitch.

Duration Control:

Timer 6 was configured to count clock cycles corresponding to the note’s duration.

I calculated the necessary delay by converting the duration (in milliseconds) into clock cycles using the formula:
delay = system_clock_frequency × duration_in_seconds.

Audio Amplification:

I used an LM386 amplifier between the GPIO pin and the speaker to ensure adequate current for sound output.





To verify the system’s performance:

PWM Output: Measured the GPIO pin output using an oscilloscope to confirm that the square wave matched the expected frequency for each note.

Full Playback Test: Played the entire song to verify that the pitch and tempo matched expectations.





The system successfully met the requirements by playing “Für Elise” with accurate pitches and timing.

Challenges included ensuring consistent timing and debugging timer register configurations, which were resolved through incremental testing and review of the MCU datasheet.




I spent approximately 10 hours on this lab, including time for debugging and testing.



This assignment was particularly enjoyable due to its combination of hardware and software challenges. For future iterations, I recommend providing more detailed starter documentation on timer register configurations to help students unfamiliar with the datasheet navigate it more efficiently.

title: Week 1 Reflection
text: To start off, I had a lot of fun on this lab! Though a lot of time was spent soldering annoyingly small SMTs, by the end of it I not only felt comfortable with soldering tiny parts, but I felt quite efficient at it! Besides that this firt lab acted as a great refresher for a lot of basic Verilog concepts such as when to us the get operater <= vs assign =, when to use alwayscomb vs always_ff, along with what the word volatile even means! I also feel like I was able to gain familiarity with lattice radiant as a software, and though I was able to incorporate modelsim to simulate expected values, I still had to comb through the results by hand. Ideally I hope that by the next lab I will be able to construct a test bench to make those simulated outputs easier to check off. I am looking forward to the next few set of labs, and am happy I got this done!
